Home Journal Office. No 107 Fulton Street.
New York. March 3. 1862.
My dear Willis,
An esteemed friend in Washington (Gen. Ward) writes
to me as follows, "Do write to Willis to speak at once
to the President, in his earnest and persuasive manner,
about the worthy Captain's (Wm Morris) promotion to the
office of Inspector General, with the rank of Colonel
in the regular Army, where he belongs, being a graduate
of West Point, and having served with honor in the
Army for several years. He earnestly desires the place,
although not up to his merits. His fine abilities, and his claims
as your son, richly deserve this recognition on the part
of the government. If Willis will do this immediately, and
urge the Captains appointment, it will help the application
made by the members of Congress from New York, if not ensure
success."
Now, my dear Willis, let me call your prompt attention
to what my friend thinks and urges. You will do it,
of course, and prey do it effectively. You are capable
of great things in these matters, and as we have both
supported the President, and aided him to the upmost of our
abilities, I hope he will allow our claim to his generous
recognition. As there are other applicants for the same office,
and none more worthy than ours, there is no time to lose
in your calling the attention of our glorious President to
this matter.
Yours most faithfully,
Geo. P. Morris
N. P. Willis Esquire

Washington City
Dr Sir
Since I left you
have been quite sick or I should have written
you before now I suffered with my hoarse
-ness after reaching home untill I had to go
through a course of medical treatment
I am now however entirely restored and enabled
to attend to my daily avocations for which I
feel very thankful to my Heavenly Father.
I feel very sorry for you on account of
your sad bereavement and think I know
how to sympathise with you as I have had
as many as 7 out of 14 of my children to
die; at one time 3 in 12 days but feel that
they are in a better world than this O; I think
I know what your companion Mrs. Licoln

bereavement and dispensation of Divine
Providence but he knows what is best for us

State Agricultural Rooms.
Columbus, O February 25th 1862
Hon. Caleb B. Smith
Secretary of the Interior
Dr Sir
Permit me to introduce o your favorable
consideration my friend Dr Norton S. Townshend of Lorain Co Ohio. Mr Townshend
is an applicant for the appointment of Chief of the Agricultural Bureau about to be
established in pursuance of a Bill introduced before Congress by Hon. Mr. Lovejoy.
Mr Townshend is a very competent man in every sense of the word - in fact in the
entire range of any acquaintance I do not know his superior or equal for the position
which he solicits. He is a graduate of the best medical school of N.Y. Paris (France)
and London (England). From his youth to the present time he has been connected with
practical agricultural operations, and is the best versed gentleman in agricultural literature
(French & English) of any acquaintance.
Should he be so fortunate as to recieve the appointment, the duties of the position
will be discharges with the utmost ability, and the appointment will give the most
unbounded satisfaction to the agricultural interest in Ohio
Respectfully
Yours truly
John H. Klippart

At a meeting of the Citizens of New York
held at the Cooper Institute in the City of
New York on Thursday Evening, March 6th 1862
the following Resolutions were unanimously
adopted:
Resolved, That inasmuch as our nationality
and democratic institutions are founded upon the
idea that "all men are created equal, endowed by
their Creator with the inalienable rights of life, liberty,
and the pursuit of happiness," whatever tends to
weaken and destroy the vital force of this idea in
the popular heart constitutes the most dangerous
and fatal enmity to the real unity, true peace,
and glory of the nation.
Resolved, That national unity does by no
means consist alone in the conservation of territorial

From Abraham Lincoln to Samuel P. Lee [Draft]1, July [4] 1863
Navy Department
Washington, D. C. July 1863
Your despatch transmitting a note from Mr. Alexander H. Stephens has been received. You will not permit Mr. Stephens to proceed to Washington, or to pass the blockade. He does not make known the subjects to which the communication in writing from Mr. Davis relates, which he bears, and seeks to deliver in person to the President, and upon which he desires to confer— Those subjects can only be Military, or not Military, or partly both. Whatever may be Military will be readily received, if offered through the well understood Military channel. Of course nothing not military other than else, will be received by the President, when offered, as in this case, in terms assuming the independence of the so-called Confederate States; and anything will be received and respectfully carefully considered by him, when offered by any influential citizen person or persons, in terms not assuming the independence of the so-called Confederate States.

From Abraham Lincoln to Samuel R. Curtis [Copy in Nicolay's Hand]1, June 8, 1863
Executive Mansion,
Washington, June 8, 1863.
My Dear Sir:
I have scarcely supposed it possible that you would entirely understand my feelings and motives in making the late change of commander for the Department of the Missouri. I enclose you a copy of a letter which I recently addressed to General Schofield and which will explain the matter in part. It became almost a matter of personal self-defense to somehow break up the state of things in Missouri. I did not mean to cast any censure upon you, nor to endorse any of the charges made against you by others. With me the presumption is still in your favor that you are honest, capable faithful and patriotic.
Yours very truly
A. Lincoln2
